summary:
Bulgaria is an EU member state that imposes no traveller-facing restrictions on gender expression. There is no criminalisation of gender identity or presentation, no statute governing which public facilities a person may use on the basis of gender, and no document, entry or border screening that turns on a visitor's gender marker. Same-sex relations have been decriminalised since 1968. Entry and visa rules are applied to foreign passports on ordinary terms, and a recorded gender raises no separate question at the border.

Legal gender recognition is effectively closed. The Supreme Court of Cassation's interpretative decision of 20 February 2023 holds that "the only meaning of the term sex should be its biological one" and that the legal system rests on "the binary existence of humankind", which bars legal gender change; the Constitutional Court's verdict on the Istanbul Convention condemned the legislation permitting it. The European Court of Human Rights found in Y.T. v Bulgaria in 2020 that refusal of legal gender recognition violates Article 8, and in December 2024 the Court confirmed that those obligations were unaffected by the 2024 revision of the gender-recognition registry; Judge Šimáčková dissented that the revision decision was over-formalistic. In September 2025 an Advocate General of the Court of Justice of the European Union, Richard de la Tour, opined that EU law precludes national legislation such as Bulgaria's that refuses a trans person identity documents matching their presented gender, and the Court concurred with that reasoning. That line of pressure is unresolved at the level of a final judgment, and a visitor whose passport carries a marker inconsistent with presentation should assume Bulgarian authorities will treat the document as issued.

Public visibility carries documented violence risk with weak state response. Hate crimes against LGBT people are frequently ignored and go uninvestigated, including the 2008 killing of a 25-year-old student in a Sofia park by a group intending to "cleanse" it of gay people, and the assault in Plovdiv on 27 September 2020 on children as young as 14 or 15 by ultra-fans of Botev acting in an anti-LGBT "cleansing action". The first Sofia Pride in 2008, with about 150 participants, was attacked with petrol bombs, rocks and glass bottles and more than 60 hooligans were arrested; the 2011 parade passed without incident only under heavy police guard; in 2017 Human Rights Watch warned that the group National Resistance was rallying counter-demonstrators to "cleanse Sofia from garbage". Order at Pride events is therefore police-dependent rather than structural.

Legislation now restricts discussion of gender identity directly. On 7 August 2024 Bulgaria's parliament amended the education law to prohibit "propaganda, promotion, or incitement" in the education system of ideas about non-traditional sexual orientation or gender identity other than the biological one; the amendment was introduced by the Revival party, backed by GERB, signed by President Rumen Radev, and in force from 16 August 2024. At municipal level the District Council of Pazardzhik voted in November 2009 to forbid the public demonstration of sexual or any other orientation; an administrative court struck it down in October 2010 on procedural grounds and upheld it on appeal in July 2011.

Anti-discrimination legislation in force since 1 January 2004 prohibits direct and indirect discrimination in housing, education and medical treatment and bans hate speech based on sexual orientation; a 2015 amendment extended coverage to "sex" as including "sex change", though gender expression and gender identity are not named explicitly. A visitor refused a room, treatment or service on that ground has a statutory basis for complaint, but the enforcement pattern described below qualifies its practical weight. Health services fall within that ban, while same-sex couples are denied the right to make medical decisions for one another.
tangentialFactors:
Institutional non-response to bias crime is long-standing rather than episodic. Amnesty International's February 2015 report "Missing the point" found that authorities consistently failed to identify and adequately investigate hate crimes: legislation existed, but bias attacks that spiked in 2013 according to the Bulgarian Helsinki Committee went unpursued, with the Sofia prosecution opening only some cases. A January 2014 government commitment to outlaw hate crimes against LGBT people was dropped by the government formed after the October 2014 elections. Heavier penalties for crimes motivated by sexual orientation were adopted on 28 July 2023, but the reporting that follows the 2020 Plovdiv assault continues to describe hate crimes as uninvestigated.

Hostility to visible LGBT events is organised and recurrent. Beyond the National Resistance counter-demonstrations, the Ataka party has protested Pride, far-right groups have advocated using brooms and shovels against attendees, billboards promoting tolerance toward same-sex couples in Varna and Burgas were vandalised in December 2018, and the Bulgarian Orthodox Church describes Pride events as a "sinful demonstration". The 2020 to 2021 period saw a rise in anti-LGBT rhetoric in which gender became a slur. ILGA-Europe ranked Bulgaria 37th of 49 European countries for LGBT rights protection in 2020.

The legal regime for same-sex couples is relevant to any visitor arriving with a partner. Article 46 of the Constitution has defined marriage as a union between a man and a woman since 1991, and although the Constitution does not bar civil unions, none exist, so same-sex couples lack inheritance, joint property and medical decision-making rights, and are barred from adopting. A Sofia court granted residency in June 2018 to an Australian woman and her French wife on the basis of the Court of Justice's Coman ruling after residency had been denied a year earlier; a Bulgarian court recognised a French same-sex marriage in 2019; a couple who married in the United Kingdom had their recognition claim rejected by the Sofia Administrative Court in January 2018, with the appeal pursued by the organisation Deystvie. In September 2023 the European Court of Human Rights held that Bulgaria's non-recognition of same-sex couples is an infringement of human rights, subject to appeals and awaiting a government response. In 2021 a Court of Justice ruling forced Bulgaria to issue an identity document to a child of a lesbian couple after it had refused a birth certificate.

Blood donation is not restricted on orientation grounds. Gay and bisexual men are not explicitly barred; a Ministry of Healthcare ordinance of 19 July 2004 sets a donor form that does not ask about orientation but requires confirmation of no HIV or STI-risk practices.
localsOnly:
Residents have no route to legal gender recognition. The Supreme Court of Cassation's interpretative decision of 20 February 2023 forecloses it on a biological reading of sex, and the Constitutional Court's Istanbul Convention verdict condemned the permitting legislation; the 2024 revision of the gender-recognition registry did not alter the European Court of Human Rights' Article 8 obligations arising from Y.T. v Bulgaria, and the Court of Justice's 2025 reasoning on identity documents remains to be applied in practice.

Intersex newborns routinely have male genitalia removed as the easier operation, and parents are rarely informed of the later harm such surgery can cause to a child's gender identity. Bulgaria has no laws concerning intersex people, and no framework governs consent, timing or disclosure.

Young LGBT people have one dedicated national support channel: the Single Step Foundation, founded in 2016, launched Bulgaria's first licensed online support chat in October 2017 for LGBTI youth, families and allies, and works specifically with young people on coming out and affirmation. Access to that support is being narrowed from the education side by the amendment in force since 16 August 2024, which bars promotion of ideas about non-biological gender identity in the education system and defines non-traditional orientation as attraction contrary to Bulgaria's legal concept of opposite sexes.

Same-sex couples cannot marry or enter a civil union, cannot adopt, and cannot make medical decisions for each other. Recognition of marriages performed abroad has been granted case by case and refused in others, so residency and property consequences for couples remain uncertain.
outOfScopeNotes:
Two court tracks are unresolved in the sources available. The Court of Justice of the European Union's reasoning in the Bulgarian identity-document case is dated to an Advocate General's opinion of September 2025 and the Court's concurrence with that reasoning, but no final judgment is recorded here; whether Bulgarian administrative practice has changed since is not sourced. The September 2023 European Court of Human Rights finding on non-recognition of same-sex couples is described as subject to appeals and awaiting a government response, with no outcome recorded.

Whether the July 2023 heavier penalties for sexual-orientation-based crimes have produced any measurable change in investigation or prosecution is not sourced. The most recent direct evidence of enforcement failure in the inventory remains the 2020 Plovdiv assault and the 2015 Amnesty International findings; a reader should treat the current investigation rate as unresolved rather than assume improvement or deterioration.

Practical police behaviour at Pride events after 2017, and any travel advisories issued by foreign ministries specifically addressing gender marker inconsistencies on passports at Bulgarian border points, are not covered by this inventory.
